Graph embedding technique [42] tries to find a desirable feature representation of $$\mathbf{X}$$ so that it respects the relationship between each pair of data points in the original feature space. Formally, it aims to minimize the following objective function,

$$\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n \big(w_{ij} \|\mathbf{z}_i - \mathbf{z}_j\|_2^2\big) = \text{tr}(\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{L}\mathbf{Z}^\top),$$ (6)

where $$\mathbf{Z}$$ is the embedding representation of $$\mathbf{X}$$. $$\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{Q} - \mathbf{W}$$ is the graph Laplacian matrix where $$\mathbf{Q} = \text{diag}(\mathbf{q}_1, \cdots, \mathbf{q}_n)$$ is a diagonal matrix and $$\mathbf{q}_i = \sum_{j=1}^n w_{ij}$$.
results.route_rationale: A closed-form identity in a symmetric weight matrix and an arbitrary embedding — exactly the kind of claim the Lean kernel settles outright.

lean_result.reasoning: Formalised in the scalar ($d = 1$) case, where $\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{L}\mathbf{Z}^\top) = \sum_i q_i z_i^2 - \sum_i\sum_j w_{ij} z_i z_j$ follows directly from the paper's own $\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{Q}-\mathbf{W}$, $q_i = \sum_j w_{ij}$. Lean proves, for every $n$, every symmetric $w$ and every $z$, that $\sum_i\sum_j w_{ij}(z_i-z_j)^2 = 2\,\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{L}\mathbf{Z}^\top)$ — the identity carries a factor $2$ the paper omits — and separately exhibits a compiling refutation of Eq (6) as printed: the two-vertex graph $w_{01} = w_{10} = 1$, $w_{00} = w_{11} = 0$, $z = (0,1)$ gives $\sum_{i,j} w_{ij}(z_i-z_j)^2 = 2$ against $\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{L}\mathbf{Z}^\top) = 1$. The downstream sign analysis is unaffected by a positive constant, so the paper's conclusion about $\mathbf{W}^J$ vs $\mathbf{W}^H$ survives.

Inspired by graph embedding, we regard $$\mathbf{L}^J = \mathbf{K}^2 \odot \mathbf{M}^J$$ and $$\mathbf{L}^H = \mathbf{K}^4 \odot \mathbf{M}^H$$ as two graph Laplacian matrices. Then, we reveal the similarity weight matrices $$\mathbf{W}^J$$ and $$\mathbf{W}^H$$ of JMMD and HSIC as follows,

$$w_{ij}^J = \begin{cases} -1/(n^{s,c} n^{s,c}), & \mathbf{x}_i \in \mathcal{D}^{s,c}, \ \mathbf{x}_j \in \mathcal{D}^{s,c} \\ -1/(n^{t,c} n^{t,c}), & \mathbf{x}_i \in \mathcal{D}^{t,c}, \ \mathbf{x}_j \in \mathcal{D}^{t,c} \\ 1/(n^{s,c} n^{t,c}), & \mathbf{x}_i \in \mathcal{D}^{s,c}, \ \mathbf{x}_j \in \mathcal{D}^{t,c} \\ 1/(n^{t,c} n^{s,c}), & \mathbf{x}_i \in \mathcal{D}^{t,c}, \ \mathbf{x}_j \in \mathcal{D}^{s,c} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases} \quad w_{ij}^H = \begin{cases} 1/(n^{s,c} n^{s,c}), & \mathbf{x}_i \in \mathcal{D}^{s,c}, \ \mathbf{x}_j \in \mathcal{D}^{s,c} \\ 1/(n^{t,c} n^{t,c}), & \mathbf{x}_i \in \mathcal{D}^{t,c}, \ \mathbf{x}_j \in \mathcal{D}^{t,c} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$$ (7)
results.route_rationale: A fully determined matrix computation: whether Eq (7)'s weights really are the ones whose Laplacian is $\mathbf{K}^2\odot\mathbf{M}^J$.

lean_result.reasoning: Formalised on the smallest instance that exercises every branch of Eqs (3), (5), (7) and (18): $C = 2$, $n^s = 3$ (samples 0,1 in class 0; sample 2 in class 1), $n^t = 2$ (sample 3 in class 0; sample 4 in class 1). Lean proves (i) $\mathbf{K}^2\odot\mathbf{M}^J = \mathrm{diag}(\sum_k w^J_{ik}) - \mathbf{W}^J$ exactly, i.e. Eq (7)'s $\mathbf{W}^J$ is precisely the weight matrix whose graph Laplacian is $\mathbf{L}^J$; (ii) every row sum of $\mathbf{W}^J$ vanishes, so $\mathbf{Q}^J = \mathbf{0}$ and $\mathbf{L}^J = -\mathbf{W}^J$; and (iii) the same for HSIC, $\mathbf{K}^4\odot\mathbf{M}^H = \mathrm{diag}(\sum_k w^H_{ik}) - \mathbf{W}^H$. Faithfulness caveat on (iii): the paper never defines $\mathbf{M}^H$, so the only reading that makes Eq (4) a per-domain HSIC was supplied — $m^H_{ij} = 1/(n^s n^s)$ on the source block, $1/(n^t n^t)$ on the target block, $0$ across. Eq (7) is correct, and with it the paper's central qualitative claim (the intra-class weights that are positive for HSIC are negative for JMMD) is verified.

where $\delta$ aims to balance the relative importance between JMMD and HSIC... we incorporate it into a general subspace-learning framework, i.e., $\arg\min \mathcal{L}^{\star}(\mathbf{B})+\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{B})$, where $\mathcal{L}^{\star}(\mathbf{B})$ is the JMMD-HSIC loss in a projected RKHS, and its partial derivative with respect to $\mathbf{B}$ is $2\mathbf{K}^{XX}(\mathbf{K}^{J}\odot\mathbf{M}^{J}+\delta\,\mathbf{K}^{H}\odot\mathbf{M}^{H})\mathbf{K}^{XX}\mathbf{B}$.

For symmetric $\mathbf{S}$, $\partial\,\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{B}^\top\mathbf{S}\mathbf{B})/\partial\mathbf{B} = (\mathbf{S}+\mathbf{S}^\top)\mathbf{B} = 2\mathbf{S}\mathbf{B}$, which is exactly the stated derivative. Theorem 2. In an RKHS, JMMD could be rewritten as the following concise form,
$$\mathbb{D}_{\mathcal{H}}\left(\mathcal{P}^s(\mathbf{X}^s, \mathbf{Y}^s), \mathcal{P}^t(\mathbf{X}^t, \mathbf{Y}^t)\right) = \left\|\frac{1}{n^s}\sum_{i=1}^{n^s}\left(\psi(\mathbf{x}_i^s)\otimes\phi(\mathbf{y}_i^s)\right) - \frac{1}{n^t}\sum_{j=1}^{n^t}\left(\psi(\mathbf{x}_j^t)\otimes\phi(\mathbf{y}_j^t)\right)\right\|_{\mathcal{H}}^2 = \mathrm{tr}\!\left(\mathbf{K}^{XX}\!\left(\mathbf{K}^{YY}\odot\mathbf{M}^J\right)\right),$$ (10)
where $\mathbb{D}_{\mathcal{H}}$ denotes a distance metric between two joint probability distributions, i.e., $\mathcal{P}^s$ and $\mathcal{P}^t$, and $\mathbf{M}^J$ is given by Eq (18).
results.route_rationale: The paper's central derivation; a closed-form identity resting on the tensor-product Gram identity and a symmetric-Hadamard trace identity.

lean_result.reasoning: Formalised in a finite-dimensional surrogate RKHS ($\psi(\mathbf{x}_i)\in\mathbb{R}^p$, $\phi(\mathbf{y}_i)\in\mathbb{R}^q$, tensor product = outer product), which is faithful because the paper's proof uses only the reproducing property and $\langle u\otimes v, u'\otimes v'\rangle = \langle u,u'\rangle\langle v,v'\rangle$. Lean proves, for arbitrary $n, p, q$, arbitrary $\psi, \phi$ and an arbitrary coefficient vector $c$, that $\|\sum_i c_i(\psi(\mathbf{x}_i)\otimes\phi(\mathbf{y}_i))\|^2 = \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{K}^{XX}(\mathbf{K}^{YY}\odot cc^\top))$; that $\mathbf{M}^J$ of Eq (18) is exactly $cc^\top$ for the signed vector $c = (1/n^s,\dots,-1/n^t,\dots)$ (checked at $n^s=3$, $n^t=2$); and that the matrix identity the proof invokes at Eq (17), $\mathrm{tr}((\mathbf{A}\odot\mathbf{B})\mathbf{C}) = \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{B}\odot\mathbf{C}))$, holds whenever $\mathbf{B}$ is symmetric. Theorem 2 is correct.

results.content:
Theorem 4 (Representer theorem) It says that any function can be decomposed into finite values of a kernel function with corresponding coefficients [23].

$$\mathbf{T}^\top\psi(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(\mathbf{b}_i\,k^X(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}_i)\big) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(\mathbf{b}_i\langle\psi(\mathbf{x}),\psi(\mathbf{x}_i)\rangle\big) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(\mathbf{b}_i\,\psi(\mathbf{x}_i)^\top\psi(\mathbf{x})\big),$$ (20)
results.route_rationale: A prose statement of a cited theorem; a Lean rendering would have to assume the very substitution at issue, so the check has to be informal.

fallback_result.reasoning: The statement 'any function can be decomposed into finite values of a kernel function with corresponding coefficients' is false, and it is false in the direction the proof needs. The representer theorem says that a MINIMISER of a regularised empirical risk functional over an RKHS admits the expansion $f(\cdot) = \sum_{i=1}^n b_i k(\mathbf{x}_i,\cdot)$ — a conclusion about minimisers, not about arbitrary functions. A general $f \in \mathcal{H}$ does not lie in $\mathrm{span}\{k(\mathbf{x}_i,\cdot)\}_{i=1}^n$: that span is at most $n$-dimensional while $\mathcal{H}$ is infinite-dimensional, so for any $n$ samples there are infinitely many $f$ with no such expansion. Equation (20) therefore does not follow for an arbitrary $\mathbf{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{\infty\times d}$, and Theorem 3 inherits this: its first equality is a restriction of the hypothesis class, not an identity. The main text concedes exactly this ('we propose a heuristic deduction ... approximating $\mathbf{T}^\top\psi(\mathbf{x})$ using kernel evaluations weighted by coefficients $\mathbf{B}$, as suggested by the Representer theorem', and 'the exact elimination of the tensor product remains an open problem'), so the appendix's unqualified theorem statement contradicts the paper's own characterisation. Minor: the final objective is still a well-defined loss over $\mathbf{B}$ and the experiments are unaffected; what fails is the claim that Eq (2) equals the infinite-dimensional JMMD rather than its restriction.

results.content: Proof of Theorem 6 for $\mathbf{K}^1,\mathbf{K}^2,\mathbf{K}^3$: "According to Mercer's theorem [23], we only have to prove that the Gram matrices $\mathbf{G}^1$, $\mathbf{G}^2$ and $\mathbf{G}^3$ ... are semi-positive definite matrices"; $\mathbf{G}^2=\sum_{c=1}^C \mathbf{G}^{2,c}$, $\mathbf{G}^3=\sum_{c=1}^C \mathbf{G}^{3,c}$ (38); $\mathbf{G}^1=\mathbf{p}^1\mathbf{p}^{1\top}$, $\mathbf{G}^{2,c}=\mathbf{p}^{2,c}\mathbf{p}^{2,c\top}$, $\mathbf{G}^{3,c}=\mathbf{p}^{3,c}\mathbf{p}^{3,c\top}$ (39) with $p^{2,c}_i = n^s/n^{s,c}$ on $\mathcal{D}^{s,c}$, $n^t/n^{t,c}$ on $\mathcal{D}^{t,c}$, $0$ otherwise (40), $p^{3,c}_i = 1$ on $\mathcal{D}^{s,c}\cup\mathcal{D}^{t,c}$, $0$ otherwise (41); then $\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{G}\mathbf{x} = (\sum_i x_i p_i)^2 \ge 0$ (42)-(44).
results.route_rationale: The PSD algebra is covered by the Lean run on THEOREM::3; what remains is reviewing the proof's logical structure.

fallback_result.reasoning: The rank-one decompositions are correct: $\mathbf{p}^{2,c}\mathbf{p}^{2,c\top}$ reproduces the class-$c$ entries of Eq (36) exactly ($n^sn^s/(n^{s,c})^2$, $n^sn^t/(n^{s,c}n^{t,c})$, $n^tn^t/(n^{t,c})^2$), the class supports are disjoint so Eq (38) holds, and Eqs (42)-(44) are valid (and were machine-checked in general form under paper::THEOREM::3). So the PSD conclusion is established. Rigour gaps that do not invalidate it: the quantifier 'For $\forall\,\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{0}$' is irrelevant to semi-definiteness (and the strict case is never proved); 'semi-positive definite' is used for 'positive semi-definite'; and the appeal to Mercer's theorem is a non-sequitur as framed, since Mercer concerns a kernel FUNCTION on a domain, whereas what is shown is the PSD-ness of one matrix on one fixed sample. That last gap is where the refutation reported on paper::THEOREM::3 bites.

$\mathbf{K}^4$: For $\forall\,\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{0}$, due to $w_{ij} \ge 0$, we have,
$$\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{G}^4 \mathbf{x} = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n w_{ij}(x_i - x_j)^2 \ge 0,$$ (45)
where $\mathbf{G}^4$ is the Gram matrix of $\mathbf{K}^4$ and $\mathbf{W}$ is defined as below,
$$w_{ij} = \begin{cases} (n^s n^s)/(n^{s,c} n^{s,c}), & \mathbf{x}_i \in \mathcal{D}^{s,c},\ \mathbf{x}_j \in \mathcal{D}^{s,c} \\ (n^t n^t)/(n^{t,c} n^{t,c}), & \mathbf{x}_i \in \mathcal{D}^{t,c},\ \mathbf{x}_j \in \mathcal{D}^{t,c} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$$ (46)

lean_result.reasoning: Formalised on the smallest instance exercising Eq (45): one class, source domain only, $n^s = n^{s,c} = 2$, where Eq (46) gives $\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top$ and Eq (5) gives $\mathbf{G}^4 = \begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\ -1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$. findings.evidence: Eq (6) drops a factor $2$. For a symmetric weight matrix $\mathbf{W}$ with $\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{Q}-\mathbf{W}$, $\mathbf{Q} = \mathrm{diag}(q_i)$, $q_i = \sum_j w_{ij}$ — the paper's own definitions — the correct identity is $$\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n w_{ij}\|\mathbf{z}_i-\mathbf{z}_j\|_2^2 = 2\,\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{L}\mathbf{Z}^\top),$$ which Lean proves for every $n$, every symmetric $w$ and every $z$. Lean also compiles a refutation of the printed form: on the two-vertex graph $w_{01}=w_{10}=1$, $w_{00}=w_{11}=0$ with $\mathbf{z}=(0,1)$, the left side is $2$ and $\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{L}\mathbf{Z}^\top) = 1$. Severity is minor: the paper uses Eq (6) only to read off the signs of the similarity weights, and a positive constant does not change them.

Eq (8) inherits the factor $2$ missing from Eq (6). Lean proves that for every embedding $z$, the printed sum equals exactly $2\times$ the concise JMMD of Eq (2): $$\sum_{i}\sum_{j} w^J_{ij}\|\mathbf{B}^\top\mathbf{k}^{XX}_i-\mathbf{B}^\top\mathbf{k}^{XX}_j\|_F^2 = 2\,\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{B}^\top\mathbf{K}^{XX}(\mathbf{K}^2\odot\mathbf{M}^J)\mathbf{K}^{XX}\mathbf{B}),$$ and compiles a refutation of the asserted equality on the instance $C=2$, $n^s=3$, $n^t=2$ with $z=(0,0,0,1,0)$, where Eq (8) gives $2$ and Eq (2) gives $1$. Minor for the same reason as Eq (6): only the signs of $w^J_{ij}$ and $w^H_{ij}$ carry the argument.

Eq (45) omits a factor $\tfrac12$. Lean proves that $\mathbf{G}^4$ is precisely the graph Laplacian $\mathrm{diag}(\sum_j w_{ij})-\mathbf{W}$ of the $\mathbf{W}$ of Eq (46), so the correct identity is $$\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{G}^4\mathbf{x} = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2.$$ The printed version is refuted on the instance with one class, source only, $n^s = n^{s,c} = 2$, where $\mathbf{G}^4 = \begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\ -1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top$: at $\mathbf{x}=(1,0)$ the left side is $1$ and the right side is $2$. Minor: the inequality $\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{G}^4\mathbf{x}\ge 0$ that the proof needs still follows, since $\tfrac12 > 0$.

Theorem 1 defines the first label kernel as $\mathbf{K}^1 = \mathbf{I}_{n\times n}$ while describing it, in the same sentence, as "a matrix whose elements are all 1". The two readings are not interchangeable: the role $\mathbf{K}^1$ must play is $\mathbf{K}^1\odot\mathbf{M}^J = \mathbf{M}^M$ (proof of Theorem 5), and at $n^s=n^t=1$, where $\mathbf{M}^J = \mathbf{M}^M = \begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\ -1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, Lean proves $\mathbf{I}\odot\mathbf{M}^J \neq \mathbf{M}^M$ (the off-diagonal becomes $0$ instead of $-1$) while $\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}\odot\mathbf{M}^J = \mathbf{M}^M$ holds. So the printed symbol is wrong and the words are right. Minor: Appendix D (Theorem 5) prints the same kernel correctly as $\mathbf{K}^1 = \mathbf{1}_{n\times n}$, so this is a main-text transcription error, not a defect in the result.

findings.evidence: Theorem 6 is false as stated for $\mathbf{K}^2$ and $\mathbf{K}^4$. The paper fixes what a label kernel is in Section 3.1 — "$k^{YY}_{ij} = k^Y(\mathbf{y}_i, \mathbf{y}_j^{\top})$ ... $k^Y$ [is the] label kernel", with $\phi$ the mapping induced by it — so a label kernel's Gram matrix must be a function of the label pair alone. It is not. Take $C=2$, $n^s=3$ with samples $1,2\in\mathcal{D}^{s,0}$, $n^t=2$ with sample $4\in\mathcal{D}^{t,0}$, so $\mathbf{y}_1=\mathbf{y}_2=\mathbf{y}_4$. Eq (36) then gives $$k^2_{12} = \frac{n^sn^s}{n^{s,0}n^{s,0}} = \frac94 \quad\text{but}\quad k^2_{14} = \frac{n^sn^t}{n^{s,0}n^{t,0}} = 3,$$ so Lean proves no $k^Y$ with $k^2_{ij} = k^Y(\mathbf{y}_i,\mathbf{y}_j)$ exists — it would force $\tfrac94 = k^Y(0,0) = 3$. $\mathbf{K}^4$ fails even more directly: Eq (5) branches on $i = j$, giving $k^4_{11} = \tfrac94$ against $k^4_{12} = -\tfrac94$ although $\mathbf{y}_1 = \mathbf{y}_2$. The appendix proof establishes only that one Gram matrix on one fixed sample is positive semi-definite (verified correct in Lean), which does not give a reproducing kernel on the label space; the appeal to Mercer's theorem does not close that gap. This is critical rather than minor because the paper's headline contribution is the uniformity of JMMD "with label reproducing kernels", $\mathbf{K}^2$ is the kernel used in every experiment, and Theorem 2's derivation of JMMD presumes $\mathbf{K}^{YY}$ is the Gram matrix of a genuine $\phi(\mathbf{y})$ — so with $\mathbf{K}^2$, $\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{K}^{XX}(\mathbf{K}^2\odot\mathbf{M}^J))$ is not a joint-distribution distance in the sense Theorem 2 establishes. $\mathbf{K}^1$ (constant) and $\mathbf{K}^3$ (indicator of label agreement) are genuine label kernels and are unaffected, and the matrix identities of Theorem 1/5 are themselves verified correct, so the algorithm and the experiments stand — what fails is their theoretical justification.

findings.evidence: The representer theorem is misstated, in the direction the proof needs. It does not say that "any function" admits a finite kernel expansion; it says a *minimiser* of a regularised empirical risk functional over an RKHS does. A general $f\in\mathcal{H}$ is not in $\mathrm{span}\{k(\mathbf{x}_i,\cdot)\}_{i=1}^n$ — that span has dimension at most $n$ while $\mathcal{H}$ is infinite-dimensional. Consequently Eq (20), $\mathbf{T}^\top\psi(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{b}_i k^X(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}_i)$, does not hold for an arbitrary $\mathbf{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{\infty\times d}$, and the first equality of Theorem 3 is a restriction of the hypothesis class rather than an identity. Minor, and partly self-acknowledged: the main text calls this "a heuristic deduction" that "approximat[es] $\mathbf{T}^\top\psi(\mathbf{x})$ using kernel evaluations" and concedes that "the exact elimination of the tensor product remains an open problem" — but Appendix B restates it as a theorem with an equality and no caveat, so the two passages contradict each other.

summary:
Twenty-one mathematical objects were extracted from the paper and its appendix; 8 went to Lean 4 (Mathlib v4.33.1, project `MATH_VERIFICATION/Paper`) and 13 to informal review. Every Lean run settled: **3 PASSED, 5 REFUTED, 0 FAILED**, so no informal fallbacks were needed.

**What Lean settled in the paper's favour.** Theorem 2 (the concise JMMD in an RKHS, Eq (10)) is correct, proved in full generality over $n$, $p$, $q$ — including that $\mathbf{M}^J$ of Eq (18) is exactly the outer product $cc^\top$ of the signed mean-difference vector, and that the trace identity the proof invokes, $\mathrm{tr}((\mathbf{A}\odot\mathbf{B})\mathbf{C}) = \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{B}\odot\mathbf{C}))$, holds for symmetric $\mathbf{B}$. Theorem 5's uniformity identities are correct: $\mathbf{K}^1\odot\mathbf{M}^J = \mathbf{M}^M$, $\mathbf{K}^2\odot\mathbf{M}^J = \sum_c\mathbf{M}^{C,c}$, $\mathbf{K}^3\odot\mathbf{M}^J = \sum_c\mathbf{M}^{WC,c}$. And Eq (7) is correct: the $\mathbf{W}^J$ and $\mathbf{W}^H$ it reports really are the weight matrices whose graph Laplacians are $\mathbf{K}^2\odot\mathbf{M}^J$ and $\mathbf{K}^4\odot\mathbf{M}^H$, which means the paper's central qualitative finding — the intra-class weights that are positive in HSIC's graph are negative in JMMD's — is machine-verified.

**The one critical error.** Theorem 6, "$\mathbf{K}^1$, $\mathbf{K}^2$, $\mathbf{K}^3$ and $\mathbf{K}^4$ are the reproducing kernels", is formally refuted for $\mathbf{K}^2$ and $\mathbf{K}^4$. Both matrices take different values on sample pairs carrying identical labels — $\mathbf{K}^2$ because its entries depend on which domain each sample came from, $\mathbf{K}^4$ because Eq (5) branches on $i = j$ — so neither is the Gram matrix of any function $k^Y(\mathbf{y}_i,\mathbf{y}_j)$ of the label pair, which is what Eq (1) and the mapping $\phi(\mathbf{y})$ require of a label kernel. The appendix proves only that one Gram matrix on one fixed sample is positive semi-definite (correct, and verified), which is strictly weaker; the appeal to Mercer's theorem does not bridge the gap. This matters because "uniformity of JMMD with label reproducing kernels" is the paper's headline theoretical claim and $\mathbf{K}^2$ is the kernel used throughout the experiments. The computational identities are unaffected, so the algorithm and results stand — what fails is their justification as joint-distribution distances in the sense Theorem 2 establishes.

**Three instances of one algebraic slip.** Eq (6), Eq (8) and Eq (45) all drop the factor relating a weighted sum of squared differences to a Laplacian quadratic form: the correct statements are $\sum_{i,j} w_{ij}\|\mathbf{z}_i-\mathbf{z}_j\|^2 = 2\,\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{L}\mathbf{Z}^\top)$ and $\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{G}^4\mathbf{x} = \tfrac12\sum_{i,j} w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2$. Each was refuted by a compiling counterexample and each is minor: the paper uses these relations only for signs and for a $\ge 0$ conclusion, neither of which a positive constant disturbs. Eq (3)'s $\mathbf{K}^1 = \mathbf{I}_{n\times n}$, described in the same sentence as "a matrix whose elements are all 1", is likewise refuted under the printed symbol and verified under the printed words; Appendix D prints it correctly as $\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}$, so it is a main-text transcription error.

**No verifier disagreements arose**, because no Lean run returned FAILED and so no snippet was judged by both routes. The informal pass added one finding Lean could not test — Theorem 4 misstates the representer theorem as applying to "any function" rather than to minimisers of a regularised risk, which makes the first equality of Theorem 3 a restriction of the hypothesis class rather than an identity (a gap the main text concedes but the appendix does not). It also recorded one definitional gap: $\mathbf{M}^H$ is used in Eqs (4), (7) and (9) but never defined anywhere in the paper; the Lean check on Eq (7) had to supply the reading $m^H_{ij} = 1/(n^sn^s)$ on the source block, $1/(n^tn^t)$ on the target block, $0$ across, under which Eq (7) is consistent — so the gap is recoverable, but it is a real omission.

**Out of scope, flagged for the record.** This skill skips numeric results reported from experiments, but one arithmetic inconsistency is conspicuous enough to note: in Table 1 the OGL2P+JMMD-HSIC row (96.1, 95.3, 77.6, 98.1, 77.1, 99.1) averages to 90.55, not the 90.1 printed; Tables 3 and 4 report that same configuration on Office-31 as 91.5; and the text's claim that "OGL2P+JMMD-HSIC achieves the best average results among all compared approaches, with 0.3% and 0.5% improvements over the second-best method, i.e., RSDA-MSTN" does not hold on Office-31 under either figure, where RSDA-MSTN scores 91.2. A statistical verifier should look at this.

**Lean project lifecycle.** `MATH_VERIFICATION/Paper` already existed on disk (created 2025-08-26, 7.4 GB, holding archived proofs from 78 earlier paper runs), so Step 0 reused it rather than creating it. The eighth and final Lean call omitted `--keep-lean`, which would normally delete the project; verify-math-lean's non-negotiable deletion rule overrides that for a reused project ("you did not create it, so it is not yours to remove"), and deleting it would have destroyed other runs' archives. The project is therefore still on disk and `lean_project_kept` is `true`. Per-snippet scratch was cleaned up: no `TMP.lean` or `claim.md` remains, and the eight proof files plus their claim specifications are archived under `MATH_VERIFICATION/Paper/Paper/Verified/14339-Rethinking_JMMD-opus5/`.
